title: Sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:30–44)
hook: he looks at the crowd with compassion and feeds five thousand

segments.voice: Yesterday, John's head: a ruler's oath at a feast, and a good man killed for it. Your line was careless words cost lives. Which promise did you keep? Day one hundred eighty-three.

The twelve come back from their travels, full of stories, and exhausted. So many people are coming and going that they don't even have time to eat. You know that week. Jesus says, come away with me to a quiet place and rest a while. They get in the boat. And the crowd sees where they're headed and runs around the shore on foot, and gets there first. The boat lands, and there they are. Thousands. Your day off, gone. Most of us would sigh. Mark tells us what Jesus felt instead. Today: sheep without a shepherd.
screen: `NO TIME EVEN TO EAT.` → `COME AWAY AND REST.` → `THE CROWD GETS THERE FIRST.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: Jesus "saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd." Moved with compassion is a gut word in Greek. It comes from the word for your insides. He felt it in his stomach. And sheep without a shepherd is an old phrase in Israel's scriptures, for a people with no one to guide or protect them. So he teaches them, for hours. Then it's late, in the middle of nowhere, and the disciples do the sensible thing: send them away to buy food. And Jesus says four words: "Give ye them to eat." You give them something. They do the math out loud. Two hundred days' wages wouldn't cover it. He asks, what have you got? Five loaves and two fish. He has everyone sit in groups on the green grass. Only Mark says green, which means spring. Then he looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the bread, and gives it to the disciples to hand out. Look up, bless, break, give: Christians hear those same four actions again at the Last Supper, and at the communion table today. Everyone eats and is satisfied. And the leftovers fill twelve baskets, one for each disciple who said send them away. Five thousand men, Mark says, not counting everyone else. Christians read it as a miracle of Jesus's power and a picture of God feeding his people. Many also notice what he did with the disciples: he didn't let them off the hook. He started with their little and put it in their hands.
screen: `MOVED WITH COMPASSION.` · `GIVE YE THEM TO EAT.` · `LOOK UP, BLESS, BREAK, GIVE.` · `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see a crowd with compassion. Settle, and breathe. Picture a crowd you'll be part of today. A commute, a store, a feed full of strangers, a waiting room. Usually we see crowds as obstacles. Try seeing them the way the text says Jesus did. Every face tired. Every face hungry for something. Many with no one looking out for them. Let the feeling land in your gut. If you pray, you can pray for that crowd. Then ask what little you have that could go into someone's hands. The bell holds the time.
Sheep without a shepherd. How Jesus saw a crowd that ruined his day off: not a nuisance, but people with no one to care for them.
Your line: you give them something. Today, when you're tempted to send a need away, see what little you have and give it. Day one hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Many Christians connect the feeding of the five thousand with communion, where bread is blessed, broken and given, and churches often run food banks and shared meals with this story in mind.

original.note: Greek: to be moved in your insides, gut-deep compassion.

trapdoor: what you thought: a picnic miracle.
what it means: Jesus feels gut-deep compassion for a leaderless crowd, and makes his disciples start with what little they have.
what a scholar hears: look up, bless, break, give: the same four verbs as the Last Supper, and sheep without a shepherd is an old phrase from Israel's scriptures.

sources.quoted: saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd

notes: 'Two hundred pennyworth' (200 denarii) glossed as 'two hundred days' wages'; confirm.
'Only Mark says green' — John 6:10 mentions 'much grass' but not green; Matthew 14:19 'grass'. Confirm the claim is precise enough.
Twelve baskets 'one for each disciple who said send them away' is an interpretive flourish; confirm or soften.
Four verbs (look up, bless, break, give) linked to the Last Supper (Mark 14:22) and communion; confirm.
Sheep without a shepherd: Numbers 27:17; Ezekiel 34:5; 1 Kings 22:17. Confirm.
